title: Kemeny rankings
description: The Kemeny rankings of an election: every ranking with the fewest disagreements with the voters (Kemeny 1959), the outcome of the Kemeny rule. Finding one is NP-hard (Bartholdi, Tovey and Trick 1989), and deciding a Kemeny winner is Theta-2-complete (Hemaspaandra, Spakowski and Vogel 2005). The loop is an implicit hitting set loop: A picks the cheapest majority preferences to overrule, C looks for a ranking that keeps all the others, and its minimal unsat cores are majority cycles (MUSes): the implicit hitting set method of MaxHS (Davies and Bacchus 2011) applied to the feedback arc sets of the majority graph. Once C finds a ranking, the cost is optimal: every ranking C has for that set is a Kemeny ranking, and the next sets of the same cost give the others. Compare the variants on the Formula 1 seasons from PrefLib.
readme:
# Project: Kemeny rankings

## Research question

The Kemeny rule (Kemeny 1959) outputs every ranking with the fewest disagreements with the
voters: its outcome is a set of rankings, not a single winner. Finding one is NP-hard (Bartholdi,
Tovey and Trick 1989; deciding a winner is Theta-2-complete, Hemaspaandra, Spakowski and Vogel
2005). Real elections are close to transitive, so few majority cycles matter. Which way of finding
them is fastest: cores of a ranking check (implicit hitting sets), cycles of three found lazily,
and how much do minimal cores matter? And what does it cost to list every optimal ranking, not
just one?

## The outcome

One solution per Kemeny ranking, as `place(X,P)` (candidate X in place P). With ties in the
majority relation there are several: the 1964 season has one Kemeny winner but 26 Kemeny
rankings, 1991 has 36. The winners are the candidates in place 1 of some solution.

## The loops

- **default**: implicit hitting sets. A picks the cheapest majority preferences to overrule (one
  per cycle found); C looks for a ranking that keeps the rest. A minimal unsat core of C is a
  cycle of majority preferences: an MUS. This is MaxHS (Davies and Bacchus 2011) on the minimum
  feedback arc set formulation of Kemeny, with the cycles generated lazily as in Baharev et al.
  (2021). Once C finds a ranking, A's cost is the optimum and every ranking C has for that set is
  a Kemeny ranking (`C.models`). The optimum is then grounded into A as a bound
  (`A.ground(bound, best)`): A proposes only sets of that cost, each is blocked after its rankings
  are listed, and the run ends exhausted when A has none left.
- **plain-cores**: the same with the cores as clasp returns them.
- **disjoint-cores**: after a cycle, its preferences are left open and C looks for a disjoint one,
  so that one optimal solve of A meets several cycles, as MaxHS solvers do.
- **lazy-transitivity**: the ordering formulation of Kemeny (a variable per pair, a constraint per
  3-cycle; Conitzer, Davenport and Kalagnanam 2006) with the 3-cycle constraints added lazily: A
  orders every pair at least cost, and each 3-cycle in its order becomes a clause from relevant/1.
  A transitive order of least cost is a Kemeny ranking; it is blocked, and with the optimum as a
  bound A runs out after the last one.
- **reference**: rankings blocked one by one (small instances only).

## Baseline

Time of a run with all solutions on clingo-wasm (`tools/bench.mjs`, suite `loops`, limit 60 s, two runs at a time) and, in brackets, the refinements added, counting the blocks of sets already listed. The small instances take under 0.2 s with every loop.

| instance | rankings | default | plain-cores | disjoint-cores | lazy-transitivity |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1964: 9 drivers | 26 | 0.0 s (5) | 0.1 s (130) | 0.0 s (5) | 0.0 s (38) |
| 1970: 9 drivers | 3 | 0.0 s (12) | 0.3 s (149) | 0.0 s (9) | 0.1 s (11) |
| 1978: 20 drivers | 10 | 0.6 s (39) | > 60 s | 0.5 s (35) | 1.3 s (37) |
| 1993: 23 drivers | 1 | 1.5 s (38) | > 60 s | 1.0 s (29) | 4.0 s (32) |
| 1991: 31 drivers | 36 | 5.0 s (82) | > 60 s | 15.0 s (77) | > 60 s |
| Latin square: 5, 65 voters | 1 | 0.0 s (6) | 0.0 s (16) | 0.0 s (5) | 0.0 s (5) |

Minimised cores matter most: on 1978 the plain cores are cycles through many candidates, and the
loop is still collecting them (thousands) after a minute. Listing the rankings costs little: the
1991 season, which no winners loop finished in two minutes (each winner needs its own optimum),
gives all 36 rankings in 5 s once the one optimum is known.

## Things to try

- Seed A with all 3-cycles at once, or stratify the hitting sets by margin.
- Combine the two refinements: a cycle core and the 3-cycles it contains.
- A view that draws the majority graph and the cycles found so far.

## How to measure

Each suite runs its variants on the instances (Campaign tab, an Advanced tab); headless:
`node tools/bench.mjs kemeny-rankings --suite loops --out rows.jsonl` and `node tools/report.mjs rows.jsonl`.
The instances tagged `slow` and `bench` (the larger F1 seasons and the Latin square) are where the loops differ;
they run in the suites, never in the tests;
the small ones are for the audit (`node tools/audit.mjs kemeny-rankings --instance all`) and the tests.
The suite `mallows` draws elections of 6 to 10 candidates. Every expected count (the number of
optimal rankings) was checked against an independent encoding with clingo's own optimisation
(`--opt-mode=optN`), and by brute force over all rankings on the instances of at most 9 candidates.

## References

- J. G. Kemeny. Mathematics without numbers. *Daedalus* 88(4):577–591, 1959.
- J. Bartholdi III, C. A. Tovey and M. A. Trick. Voting schemes for which it can be difficult to tell who won the election. *Social Choice and Welfare* 6(2):157–165, 1989.
- E. Hemaspaandra, H. Spakowski and J. Vogel. The complexity of Kemeny elections. *Theoretical Computer Science* 349(3):382–391, 2005. doi:10.1016/j.tcs.2005.08.031.
- J. Davies and F. Bacchus. Solving MAXSAT by solving a sequence of simpler SAT instances. *CP 2011*, LNCS 6876, 225–239.
- A. Baharev, H. Schichl, A. Neumaier and T. Achterberg. An exact method for the minimum feedback arc set problem. *ACM Journal of Experimental Algorithmics* 26, article 1.4, 2021.
- V. Conitzer, A. Davenport and J. Kalagnanam. Improved bounds for computing Kemeny rankings. *AAAI 2006*, 620–626.
- N. Mattei and T. Walsh. PrefLib: a library for preferences. *ADT 2013*, LNCS 8176, 259–270. Data: dataset 00052 (Formula 1 seasons), https://www.preflib.org.

fragments.name: shared
fragments.text:
% The election is the instance (Instances tab). ballot(V,(A,B,...)): voter V ranks A first,
% B second, and so on; count(V,N) (optional): N voters cast this ballot, as in PrefLib's
% "N: a,b,...". Ballots of 3 to 12 candidates are read below; for more, give rank(V,P,X).
rank(V,1,A;V,2,B;V,3,C) :- ballot(V,(A,B,C)).
rank(V,1,A;V,2,B;V,3,C;V,4,D) :- ballot(V,(A,B,C,D)).
rank(V,1,A;V,2,B;V,3,C;V,4,D;V,5,E) :- ballot(V,(A,B,C,D,E)).
rank(V,1,A;V,2,B;V,3,C;V,4,D;V,5,E;V,6,F) :- ballot(V,(A,B,C,D,E,F)).
rank(V,1,A;V,2,B;V,3,C;V,4,D;V,5,E;V,6,F;V,7,G) :- ballot(V,(A,B,C,D,E,F,G)).
rank(V,1,A;V,2,B;V,3,C;V,4,D;V,5,E;V,6,F;V,7,G;V,8,H) :- ballot(V,(A,B,C,D,E,F,G,H)).
rank(V,1,A;V,2,B;V,3,C;V,4,D;V,5,E;V,6,F;V,7,G;V,8,H;V,9,I) :- ballot(V,(A,B,C,D,E,F,G,H,I)).
rank(V,1,A;V,2,B;V,3,C;V,4,D;V,5,E;V,6,F;V,7,G;V,8,H;V,9,I;V,10,J) :- ballot(V,(A,B,C,D,E,F,G,H,I,J)).
rank(V,1,A;V,2,B;V,3,C;V,4,D;V,5,E;V,6,F;V,7,G;V,8,H;V,9,I;V,10,J;V,11,K) :- ballot(V,(A,B,C,D,E,F,G,H,I,J,K)).
rank(V,1,A;V,2,B;V,3,C;V,4,D;V,5,E;V,6,F;V,7,G;V,8,H;V,9,I;V,10,J;V,11,K;V,12,L) :- ballot(V,(A,B,C,D,E,F,G,H,I,J,K,L)).
% rank(V,P,X): voter V puts candidate X in place P.
cand(X) :- rank(_,_,X).
#defined count/2.
votes(V,N) :- rank(V,1,_), N = #max { 1; M : count(V,M) }.
% n(X,Y,N): N voters prefer X to Y.
n(X,Y,N) :- cand(X), cand(Y), X != Y, N = #sum { W,V : rank(V,I,X), rank(V,J,Y), I < J, votes(V,W) }.
% edge(X,Y,M): a majority prefers X to Y, by a margin of M votes.
edge(X,Y,N-K) :- n(X,Y,N), n(Y,X,K), N > K.
% Kemeny: a ranking pays, for every pair, the voters who disagree with it. Every pair costs
% at least its minority, base/1 in total; going against a majority preference of margin M
% costs M more. So w(X,Y,M) is the margin, and the Kemeny score of a ranking is base plus the
% margins of the majority preferences it goes against.
w(X,Y,M) :- edge(X,Y,M).
base(S) :- S = #sum { K,X,Y : n(X,Y,N), n(Y,X,K), K <= N, X < Y ; N,X,Y : n(X,Y,N), n(Y,X,K), N < K, X < Y }.
fragments.description: The election: pairwise counts, majority margins and the weights w/3 of the rule. Added to every solver.

fragments.name: hitting
fragments.text:
% A candidate: the majority preferences that a ranking goes against (rev), at the least cost.
% The refinements say which ones must be reversed: one of every majority cycle found so far.
{ rev(X,Y) : edge(X,Y,_) }.
% The cost: the weights of the reversed majority preferences.
#minimize { W,X,Y : rev(X,Y), w(X,Y,W) }.
#show rev/2.

#program bound(b).
% Once the optimum b is known (A.ground(bound, b)): every set costs exactly b (none costs less,
% as b is the optimum). A then runs out after the last cheapest set, and the run is exhausted.
:- #sum { W,X,Y : rev(X,Y), w(X,Y,W) } != b.
fragments.description: Solver A: a winner and the majority preferences to reverse, of least total weight.

fragments.name: glue
fragments.text:
% The check reads which majority preferences the candidate reverses.
glue(rev(X,Y)) :- edge(X,Y,_).
fragments.description: Link G: the reversed majority preferences.

fragments.name: order
fragments.text:
% A ranking (above/2: a strict linear order of the candidates) ...
{ above(X,Y) } :- cand(X), cand(Y), X < Y.
above(Y,X) :- cand(X), cand(Y), X < Y, not above(X,Y).
:- above(X,Y), above(Y,Z), above(Z,X).
% ... that keeps every majority preference the candidate does not reverse. There is none
% exactly when the kept preferences contain a cycle; a minimal unsat core is such a cycle.
:- edge(X,Y,_), not rev(X,Y), not above(X,Y).
% The outcome: place(X,P), candidate X in place P of the ranking.
place(X,N+1) :- cand(X), N = #count { Y : above(Y,X) }.
#show place/2.
fragments.description: Solver C: a ranking that keeps every majority preference the candidate does not reverse.

fragments.name: tournament
fragments.text:
% A candidate: an order of every pair of candidates (a tournament), which need not be
% transitive: the check finds the cycles, and each refinement removes one.
{ above(X,Y) } :- cand(X), cand(Y), X < Y.
above(Y,X) :- cand(X), cand(Y), X < Y, not above(X,Y).
% The cost: the weights of the majority preferences the order goes against.
#minimize { W,X,Y : w(X,Y,W), above(Y,X) }.
% The outcome, once the order is transitive: place(X,P), candidate X in place P.
place(X,N+1) :- cand(X), N = #count { Y : above(Y,X) }.
#show place/2.

#program bound(b).
% Once the optimum b is known (A.ground(bound, b)): every order costs exactly b.
:- #sum { W,X,Y : w(X,Y,W), above(Y,X) } != b.
fragments.description: Solver A of the variant lazy-transitivity: a winner and an order of every pair, of least weight.

fragments.name: triangle
fragments.text:
% A counterexample: three candidates that the order puts in a cycle. A ranking orders a
% triple transitively, so one of the three pairs must turn round.
1 { cyc(X,Y,Z) : cand(X), cand(Y), cand(Z), X < Y, X < Z, Y != Z } 1.
:- cyc(X,Y,Z), not above(X,Y).
:- cyc(X,Y,Z), not above(Y,Z).
:- cyc(X,Y,Z), not above(Z,X).
relevant(above(X,Y)) :- cyc(X,Y,Z).
relevant(above(Y,Z)) :- cyc(X,Y,Z).
relevant(above(Z,X)) :- cyc(X,Y,Z).
#show cyc/3.
fragments.description: Solver C of the variant lazy-transitivity: three candidates in a cycle.

fragments.name: glue_above
fragments.text:
% The check reads the order of every pair.
glue(above(X,Y)) :- cand(X), cand(Y), X != Y.
fragments.description: Link G of the variants lazy-transitivity and reference: the order of every pair.

fragments.name: transitive
fragments.text:
% The blocking loop's candidates are rankings: the order is transitive.
:- above(X,Y), above(Y,Z), above(Z,X).
fragments.description: Solver A of the variant reference: the order is a ranking.

fragments.name: better
fragments.text:
% A counterexample: another ranking r/2 that goes against majority preferences of a smaller
% total weight than the candidate ranking.
{ r(X,Y) } :- cand(X), cand(Y), X < Y.
r(Y,X) :- cand(X), cand(Y), X < Y, not r(X,Y).
:- r(X,Y), r(Y,Z), r(Z,X).
:- #sum { W,X,Y : w(X,Y,W), r(Y,X) ; -W,X,Y : w(X,Y,W), above(Y,X) } >= 0.
#show r/2.
fragments.description: Solver C of the variant reference: a ranking that goes against less.

loop.text:
solver A = shared + hitting
solver C = shared + order
link   G = A -> C via shared + glue

# Implicit hitting sets (MaxHS: Davies and Bacchus 2011) for the Kemeny rankings. A ranking goes
# against some majority preferences; a best ranking goes against a cheapest set of them that
# meets every cycle of the majority graph (a minimum feedback arc set). The cycles are generated
# lazily, as in Baharev, Schichl, Neumaier and Achterberg (2021): A proposes a cheapest set of
# majority preferences to go against that meets every cycle found so far; its cost is a lower
# bound. C looks for a ranking that keeps all the other majority preferences. Found: the bound is
# the optimum, and every ranking C has for this set is a Kemeny ranking (it cannot go against
# less). The set is blocked; from then on A proposes only sets of the optimal cost (the bound), and
# the loop ends when there is none left.
best = none
loop:
    M = A.solve(optimal)
    if not M: stop
    track lower = M.cost
    if C.solve(assume G(M)):
        if best == none:
            log "Kemeny score", M.value(base/1) + M.cost
            best = M.cost
            A.ground(bound, best)            # from now on, only sets of the optimal cost
        for X in C.models(assume G(M)):
            accept X                         # a Kemeny ranking: place(X,P)
        A.add(G.block(M))                    # the next set of preferences to go against
    else:
        # a minimal unsat core is a cycle of kept majority preferences (an MUS):
        # the ranking must go against one of them
        A.add(C.core.minimal.on(G))
        count cycles

% Eight voters, five candidates, no Condorcet winner: the majority prefers b to e, e to d and
% d to b. The four rules of the Voting group pick four different sets of winners here.
ballot(1,(e,d,b,a,c)).  count(1,3).
ballot(2,(b,e,d,c,a)).
ballot(3,(a,d,b,e,c)).
ballot(4,(d,b,c,a,e)).
ballot(5,(a,b,e,c,d)).  count(5,2).

% The Condorcet paradox: each candidate loses to another one two votes to one, so every
% rule ties all three.
ballot(1,(a,b,c)).
ballot(2,(b,c,a)).
ballot(3,(c,a,b)).

% A Condorcet winner, b, which beats every other candidate head to head although a and c have
% more first places. All four rules pick it alone.
ballot(1,(a,b,c,d)).  count(1,2).
ballot(2,(c,b,d,a)).  count(2,2).
ballot(3,(b,d,a,c)).

generators.name: election-mallows
generators.description: v voters over the first m of the candidates a..j, each ranking them by a Mallows model around a, b, c, ... with dispersion phi/1000 (1000 = impartial culture).
generators.text:
% election-mallows: v voters over the candidates a, b, c, ... (the first m, at most 10); voter V
% puts candidate I in place @mallows(m, phi, I, V) of a Mallows ranking around a, b, c, ...
% (dispersion phi/1000: 0 = everyone agrees, 1000 = impartial culture).
name(1,a;2,b;3,c;4,d;5,e;6,f;7,g;8,h;9,i;10,j).
voter(1..v).
rank(V,@mallows(m,phi,I,V),X) :- voter(V), name(I,X), I <= m.
#show rank/3.

generators.name: election-latin
generators.description: A Latin square: the m cyclic shifts of the ranking a, b, c, ..., each cast by lo to hi voters. No Condorcet winner unless the counts are lopsided; large Dodgson and Young scores.
generators.text:
% election-latin: the m cyclic shifts of the ranking a, b, c, ... (m at most 10), shift S cast
% by @int(lo, hi, S) voters. Every candidate is in every place once, so the counts decide.
name(1,a;2,b;3,c;4,d;5,e;6,f;7,g;8,h;9,i;10,j).
shift(0..m-1).
rank(S+1,P,X) :- shift(S), P = 1..m, name(I,X), I = (P - 1 + S) \ m + 1.
count(S+1,@int(lo,hi,S)) :- shift(S).
#show rank/3.
#show count/2.

variants.name: plain-cores
variants.note: The cores as clasp returns them (C.core), not minimised: longer cycles, weaker clauses.

loop.text:
solver A = shared + hitting
solver C = shared + order
link   G = A -> C via shared + glue

# Implicit hitting sets (MaxHS: Davies and Bacchus 2011) for the Kemeny rankings. A ranking goes
# against some majority preferences; a best ranking goes against a cheapest set of them that
# meets every cycle of the majority graph (a minimum feedback arc set). The cycles are generated
# lazily, as in Baharev, Schichl, Neumaier and Achterberg (2021): A proposes a cheapest set of
# majority preferences to go against that meets every cycle found so far; its cost is a lower
# bound. C looks for a ranking that keeps all the other majority preferences. Found: the bound is
# the optimum, and every ranking C has for this set is a Kemeny ranking (it cannot go against
# less). The set is blocked; from then on A proposes only sets of the optimal cost (the bound), and
# the loop ends when there is none left.
best = none
loop:
    M = A.solve(optimal)
    if not M: stop
    track lower = M.cost
    if C.solve(assume G(M)):
        if best == none:
            log "Kemeny score", M.value(base/1) + M.cost
            best = M.cost
            A.ground(bound, best)            # from now on, only sets of the optimal cost
        for X in C.models(assume G(M)):
            accept X                         # a Kemeny ranking: place(X,P)
        A.add(G.block(M))                    # the next set of preferences to go against
    else:
        # a minimal unsat core is a cycle of kept majority preferences (an MUS):
        # the ranking must go against one of them
        A.add(C.core.on(G))
        count cycles

variants.name: disjoint-cores
variants.note: MaxHS with disjoint cores: after each cycle its edges are left open and C looks for another one before A solves again.

loop.text:
solver A = shared + hitting
solver C = shared + order
link   G = A -> C via shared + glue

# Implicit hitting sets (MaxHS: Davies and Bacchus 2011) with disjoint cores, as MaxHS solvers
# collect them, for the Kemeny rankings: after a cycle, its edges are left open and C looks for
# another cycle that shares none of them, so that one optimal solve of A meets several at once.
best = none
loop:
    M = A.solve(optimal)
    if not M: stop
    track lower = M.cost
    E = G(M)
    found = 0
    loop:
        X = C.solve(assume E)
        if X: break
        K = C.core.minimal
        A.add(K.on(G))                       # one cycle more to break
        count cycles
        found = found + 1
        for a in K:                          # keep its edges open, look for a disjoint cycle
            E = E.without(a)
    if found == 0:
        if best == none:
            log "Kemeny score", M.value(base/1) + M.cost
            best = M.cost
            A.ground(bound, best)            # from now on, only sets of the optimal cost
        for X in C.models(assume G(M)):
            accept X
        A.add(G.block(M))

variants.name: lazy-transitivity
variants.note: Conitzer, Davenport and Kalagnanam: the order of every pair at least cost, transitivity added lazily, one 3-cycle at a time (clauses from relevant/1).

loop.text:
solver A = shared + tournament
solver C = shared + triangle
link   G = A -> C via shared + glue_above

# Lazy transitivity: the ordering formulation (one variable per pair, a constraint per
# 3-cycle; Conitzer, Davenport and Kalagnanam 2006) with the 3-cycle constraints added only
# when violated. A orders every pair at the least cost but without transitivity; C finds a
# triple in a cycle, and the clause from its three relevant pairs says that one of them must
# turn round. An order without a cycle is a ranking of least cost: a Kemeny ranking. It is
# blocked; from then on A proposes only orders of that cost (the bound), until none is left.
best = none
loop:
    M = A.solve(optimal)
    if not M: stop
    track lower = M.cost
    X = C.solve(assume G(M))
    if X:
        A.add(G.clause(M, X))            # one pair of the cycle must turn round
        count triangles
    else:
        if best == none:
            log "Kemeny score", M.value(base/1) + M.cost
            best = M.cost
            A.ground(bound, best)            # from now on, only orders of the optimal cost
        accept M
        A.add(G.block(M))

variants.name: reference
variants.note: The blocking loop: rankings with each refuted ranking blocked on its own. Small instances only.

loop.text:
solver A = shared + tournament + transitive
solver C = shared + better
link   G = A -> C via shared + glue_above

# The blocking loop: A proposes a ranking; C looks for a ranking that goes against less. A
# refuted ranking is blocked on its own; a ranking without a better one is a Kemeny ranking.
loop:
    M = A.solve()
    if not M: stop
    X = C.solve(assume G(M))
    if X:
        A.add(G.block(M))
    else:
        accept M
        A.add(G.block(M))
